title: Horse series: Grey Eagle and Wagner at the Oakland Course
summary: In 1839 Kentucky's Grey Eagle met Virginia-bred Wagner, ridden by the enslaved jockey Cato, in two four-mile-heat races at Louisville's Oakland Course. Wagner won both, and Grey Eagle broke down in the last heat.
bodyMarkdown:
In the fall of 1839 Louisville's Oakland Course staged what the turf press called the most important race ever run west of the Alleghenies. Kentucky's young [Grey Eagle](/people/#grey-eagle-horse) met [Wagner](/people/#wagner-horse), a seasoned horse from Virginia, and an enslaved jockey named [Cato](/people/#cato-jockey) became one of the best-known riders in the country.

## The course

The Oakland Course opened in 1832 on about [55 acres at today's Seventh Street and Magnolia Avenue](https://brokensidewalk.com/2017/lost-race-tracks/), in what is now Old Louisville. It had a three-story clubhouse and stables for 120 horses, but by 1839 it was struggling, and its backers hoped a great match would fill the stands.

## Two champions

Grey Eagle was [foaled near Lexington on April 20, 1835](https://archive.org/stream/americanturfregi14skin#page/174/mode/1up), a gray colt by Woodpecker out of Ophelia. In 1838 he won at two-mile heats at Oakland, and Kentuckians called him the best horse in the state. He had never run four-mile heats.

Wagner, a golden chestnut with white hind feet, was bred in Brunswick County, Virginia, and foaled in 1834 and [sold at three to a Baltimore owner for $5,000](https://archive.org/stream/americanturfregi14skin#page/367/mode/1up). He had won races a thousand miles apart, most of them at four-mile heats.

## September 30

The first meeting was a sweepstakes for ten subscribers at $2,000 each, half forfeit, plus the stand receipts; the purse was reported at [$14,000](https://nkaa.uky.edu/nkaa/items/show/2105). It was the best two of three four-mile heats. About 10,000 people came, and bets were made in dollars and in enslaved people. Grey Eagle, ridden by a white jockey, lost both heats to Wagner, in 7:48 and 7:44.

## October 5

Kentucky wanted another chance. Visitors came from as far as the Atlantic seaboard, and [Henry Clay](/people/#henry-clay) led a delegation from Lexington. Five days later the horses met again for a $1,500 Jockey Club purse. Grey Eagle won the first heat in 7:51.

Wagner took the second by barely a neck in 7:43, running the last three miles in 5:35 with both jockeys using whip and spur. In the third heat Grey Eagle [broke down in the second mile](https://archive.org/stream/americanturfregi14skin#page/176/mode/1up). He never raced again and went to stud in 1840.

## Cato

The turf editor who described the races praised Cato's coolness and presence of mind. Legend says the victories won him his freedom. Historians are less sure: a winning jockey was worth more to his owner, though the [same editor wrote that Cato was free](https://www.19thc-artworldwide.org/autumn13/dallow-on-edward-troye-s-equine-paintings) by the first race. He kept riding for Wagner's stable.

## Kentucky today

The painter [Edward Troye](/people/#edward-troye) painted both horses, and engravings after his pictures ran in the American Turf Register in 1843; the Wagner plate shows Cato at the horse's head. The course closed in the 1850s, and the Old Louisville neighborhood grew over the ground. The map pin is an approximate point at Seventh and Magnolia.
